This may be a bit personal, but if you don't mind me asking, why did you become a teacher? And why do you keep doing it?

I only ask because I'm thinking about getting into it (with the goal of starting my own "school" or tuition program of sorts). Back when I was thinking about what to do after school, I figured that if I had the skill-set to teach, I'd be much better off in the corporate world managing and training employees, or going down a STEM path, and becoming an engineer. I was very good at tutoring (very in demand, charged a fairly high rate, had to turn clients (kids and their parents) down), but never really considered teaching because of the low pay compared to other fields.

I'm a career changer. I worked in marketing and business development for many years. I got caught in the downsizing of our industrial base at a time when our children were small. I stayed home with them for a number of years, and then returned to work when college bills hit. The economy was horrible and getting back into my prior field was a big uphill climb, so I considered my options. Teaching isn't a perfect fit. Long hours, low pay, and dealing with the educational establishment are the chief downsides. A greater measure of job security (after a few years), a fair bit of day-to-day autonomy, and the opportunity to be with young people are the upsides. It's never boring, and there is satisfaction that comes with seeing students learn to think. I love science, and seeing youngsters in the lab is really a kick. At this point I keep doing it because I'm tenured and have jumped through all the hoops to be set for a while with qualifications. Retirement isn't too far off though because there is just so much good stuff to do and see, and summer is too short. My work hours during the year are excessive, and work-life balance is out of whack. Conscientious teachers put in very long hours, especially in technical fields where there are labs to set up and take down. I teach five classes, in addition to internal subbing for one period and supervising a homeroom. Of the five classes I teach, only two are the same course. I have ~125 students ranging from Freshmen to Seniors, lowest academic level to AP, and covering two core sciences. Add in some kids with learning disabilities and the workload is intense. People sometimes think teachers are done working at 3:00 or so. That's only the end of the school day. From there we deal with grading, lesson prep, long-term planning, communication (with admin, students and parents), etc, etc). It's not unusual for me to be in school from 6:30-4:00 and then do more work at home in the evening. Unit planning slides into the weekend. Think carefully about your options. It can be very rewarding, but go in with your eyes open.
